text: Giulio Carlo Argan (17 May 1909 – 12 November 1992) was an Italian art historian, critic, and politician. Born in Turin, he studied at the University of Turin and graduated in 1931. In 1928, he joined the National Fascist Party and, in the 1930s, worked for the National Antiquity and Arts Directorate, first in Turin, then in Modena, and later in Rome, where he contributed to the establishment of the Istituto Superiore per la Conservazione ed il Restauro and directed the magazine Le Arti. His career advanced through his friendship with Cesare Maria De Vecchi, who was the national Minister of Education at the time. In 1938, he published a manual of art for high schools, and during the 1940s, he collaborated with the magazine Primato, founded and directed by Giuseppe Bottai, a fellow Fascist leader. After World War II, he taught at universities in Palermo and, starting in 1959, in Rome. He co-founded the publishing house Il Saggiatore and served on the Superior Council of Antiquities and Fine Arts (the predecessor of the Ministry of Culture), a position he held until 1974. In 1968, he published his most renowned work, Storia dell'Arte Italiana (History of Italian Art). In 1973, he founded the Rome ISIA, Italy's oldest institution dedicated to industrial design. He served as the first Communist mayor of Rome from 1976 to 1979 and was elected a Foreign Honorary Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1992. He died in Rome.
